topic: Philosophy of Religion: Religious Experience, Problem of Evil
subject: religious-studies

items.q: What distinction matters for the free will defence to the problem of evil?
items.correct: Between moral evil (caused by free human choices) and natural evil (earthquakes, disease) — the free will defence directly addresses moral evil but struggles with natural evil, which isn't a product of free choice.
items.misconception: The free will defence solves all forms of evil at once.
items.random_wrong: Natural evil means evil that is good for nature.
items.why: Students apply the free will defence to all evil. The challenge of natural evil is precisely that no one chose it, requiring other theodicies (Augustinian fallen world, Irenaean soul-making) to address it.

items.q: What is the problem of evil?
items.correct: If God is all-loving, all-knowing and all-powerful, why does evil and suffering exist? Logically, all four cannot be true together without explanation.
items.misconception: It is the question of whether evil people will go to hell.
items.random_wrong: It is the question of whether the devil really exists.
items.why: Students treat it as a moral or eschatological question. It is actually a logical challenge to classical theism — and the central problem theodicies try to solve.

items.correct: Five distinct arguments for God's existence: from motion, causation, contingency, gradation of being, and final causes/teleology — collectively forming Aquinas's natural theology, not a single argument.
items.misconception: Aquinas's Five Ways are five steps of one cosmological argument.
items.random_wrong: Aquinas's Five Ways are five Christian sacraments.
items.why: Each Way is a self-standing argument with different structure. Students treat them as a single chain, missing that Aquinas offered multiple independent routes — the failure of one doesn't undermine the others.

items.q: Does Swinburne's principle of credulity make religious experiences immune to challenge?
items.correct: No — it gives initial evidential weight to how things seem, but is defeated by special considerations: unreliability of the subject, circumstances like drugs, or strong background evidence against the claim.
items.misconception: Swinburne's principle means we must accept every reported religious experience as definitely genuine.
items.random_wrong: Swinburne's principle says experiences only count if they happen in church.
items.why: Swinburne builds the defeaters into the principle itself. Presenting it as blanket credulity makes it a strawman; the live debate is whether the defeaters apply to religious cases generally.

items.q: In the Augustinian theodicy, did God create evil?
items.correct: No — God created everything good; evil is a privation of good that entered creation through the free turning-away of angels and humans, so responsibility lies with creatures.
items.misconception: Augustine says God deliberately created evil to test human beings.
items.random_wrong: Augustine says evil was created by a second, evil god.
items.why: Privatio boni plus the free fall of creatures is precisely Augustine's way of keeping God's creation wholly good. His Manichaean past made him especially keen to deny any co-eternal evil power.
Correct answer: Aquinas. “Anselm” sounds right because it borrows the language of the topic — but it fails this question. Re-read the notes on why.
The answer examiners want is: Hume. “Descartes” is the distractor this question was built around — if it tempted you, that's the exact gap to close.

items.q: How many of Aristotle's causes are there?
items.why: The real figure is 4 causes. The wrong options cluster deliberately close — anchor the exact number to one concrete fact so it can't drift.
